territories.title: Society
territories.summary: Politics, economics, institutions, law, technology adoption, media, and social organization.

branches.title: Economics
branches.summary: Schools, models, crises, institutions, measures, policy regimes, and tradeoffs.

maps.title: Economic schools
maps.subtitle: A draft map of major economic traditions by what each thinks economies are made of.
maps.question: What does each school think economies are, and what problem is it trying to solve?
maps.summary: This starter map organizes economic schools by explanatory stance: production, class conflict, marginal choice, aggregate demand, market process, and institutions or behavior.

groups.title: Classical political economy
groups.stance: Economies are systems of production, labor, land, capital, prices, and trade shaped by social order.
groups.centralClaim: Wealth grows through specialization, markets, productivity, and the allocation of surplus across classes.
groups.whyItMatters: Classical economics created the base vocabulary for markets, labor, value, rent, trade, and growth.

contributors.name: Adam Smith
contributors.reason: Connected division of labor, market coordination, moral sentiment, and political economy into a durable frame.

contributors.name: David Ricardo
contributors.reason: Formalized rent, comparative advantage, and distribution among wages, profits, and land.

texts.title: Principles of Political Economy and Taxation

objections: It can understate power, monopoly, colonial extraction, and unpaid labor.
Labor-value language became difficult to reconcile with later marginal price theory.
Its broad social frame can be less mathematically precise than later schools.

groups.title: Marxian economics
groups.stance: Capitalist economies are historical systems organized by class power, exploitation, accumulation, and crisis.
groups.centralClaim: The wage relation hides extraction of surplus value, and capitalism tends toward instability and conflict.
groups.whyItMatters: It makes power, ownership, labor, ideology, and crisis central instead of treating markets as neutral exchange systems.

contributors.name: Karl Marx
contributors.reason: Built a theory of capitalism around labor, value, class struggle, accumulation, and historical change.

contributors.name: Rosa Luxemburg
contributors.reason: Linked accumulation to expansion, imperialism, and the political pressure of capitalism beyond the factory.

objections: Critics dispute labor value theory and its predictive claims.
State socialist experiments raised practical objections about planning, incentives, and political control.
Some versions can reduce culture, law, and institutions too strongly to class interest.

groups.title: Neoclassical economics
groups.stance: Economies can be modeled as choices under scarcity, where prices coordinate marginal tradeoffs.
groups.centralClaim: Value emerges from marginal utility, constraints, preferences, and equilibrium among optimizing agents.
groups.whyItMatters: It became the dominant toolkit for microeconomics, welfare analysis, price theory, and formal policy modeling.

contributors.name: William Stanley Jevons
contributors.reason: Helped shift value theory from labor and cost toward marginal utility and mathematical reasoning.

contributors.name: Alfred Marshall
contributors.reason: Stabilized the tools of partial equilibrium, supply and demand, elasticity, and marginal analysis.

objections: It can over-idealize rationality, information, equilibrium, and representative agents.
Power, institutions, ecology, and history can appear as external complications.
Formal elegance can hide fragile assumptions.

groups.title: Keynesian economics
groups.stance: Economies can settle into bad equilibria when aggregate demand, expectations, money, and investment fail.
groups.centralClaim: Markets do not automatically restore full employment quickly, so public policy can stabilize demand and confidence.
groups.whyItMatters: It reshaped macroeconomics, fiscal policy, central banking debates, and crisis response.

contributors.name: John Maynard Keynes
contributors.reason: Reframed unemployment, money, investment, uncertainty, and demand as central macroeconomic problems.

texts.title: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

contributors.name: Joan Robinson
contributors.reason: Extended imperfect competition and challenged simple equilibrium stories inside and outside Keynesian economics.

objections: Critics argue stimulus can create inflation, debt pressure, or political dependence.
Some models rely on policy timing and knowledge governments may not have.
New classical critics challenged its treatment of expectations.

groups.title: Austrian economics
groups.stance: Economies are discovery processes driven by entrepreneurship, dispersed knowledge, prices, and time.
groups.centralClaim: Market prices coordinate knowledge no planner can fully possess, and intervention can distort capital and signals.
groups.whyItMatters: It sharpens questions about information, spontaneous order, money, business cycles, and centralized planning.

contributors.name: Carl Menger
contributors.reason: Grounded value in subjective use and helped launch marginalist thinking from an Austrian line.

contributors.name: Friedrich Hayek
contributors.reason: Argued that prices communicate dispersed knowledge and that planning faces deep information limits.

texts.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society

objections: Its policy conclusions can understate market failures, public goods, and inequality.
Some claims resist formal testing or macro measurement.
Its anti-planning frame can become too broad for mixed economies.

groups.title: Institutional and behavioral economics
groups.stance: Real economies are shaped by institutions, norms, bounded rationality, psychology, law, and collective action.
groups.centralClaim: To explain economic behavior, models must include the rules and mental shortcuts that structure choice.
groups.whyItMatters: This family repairs overly abstract models by bringing in organizations, culture, cognition, and governance.

contributors.name: Thorstein Veblen
contributors.reason: Treated habits, status, business power, and institutions as central to economic behavior.

texts.title: The Theory of the Leisure Class

contributors.name: Daniel Kahneman
contributors.reason: Brought cognitive bias, heuristics, and empirical psychology into economic judgment and choice.

contributors.name: Elinor Ostrom
contributors.reason: Showed how communities can govern shared resources through rules beyond simple state or market binaries.

objections: The family is broad and can become a toolbox rather than one unified theory.
Institutional detail can reduce portability across contexts.
Behavioral findings can be hard to scale into full macroeconomic theory.

relations.note: Marxian economics inherits classical concerns with labor, value, and surplus, then reframes them through class conflict.
Neoclassical economics shifts the center from production and class distribution to marginal choice and equilibrium.
Keynesian economics challenges the idea that markets automatically clear quickly at full employment.
They disagree over policy intervention, capital distortion, knowledge limits, and the causes of cycles.
Institutional and behavioral work addresses assumptions about rationality, rules, and context in standard models.
Both care about local knowledge and real-world rules, but they emphasize different institutional lessons.
